analysis.one_liner: Blocks royalty relief for oil and gas drilling on federal land when market prices are high.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: When the federal government leases land or offshore seabed for oil and gas drilling, companies pay royalties — a share of the value of what they pump — to the Treasury. In some leases, especially deep-water offshore ones, the government grants 'royalty relief': it suspends the royalty payments, often to encourage expensive drilling. This bill would require the Interior Secretary to attach price limits to that relief for any new lease, so that a company could not keep skipping royalty payments once oil or gas prices were high. It also reaffirmed the Secretary's existing power to apply price thresholds to leases under a 1995 deep-water relief law.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal and state treasuries — and by extension taxpayers — gain if the bill passes, because drilling companies would have to start paying royalties on new leases once energy prices rose above a threshold, instead of pumping royalty-free during price spikes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Interior Secretary to place market-price limits on any royalty relief granted in new oil and gas leases on federal land, including offshore submerged lands, so relief ends when prices are high.

It reaffirms the Secretary's statutory authority to vary royalty suspensions by price for leases under the Outer Continental Shelf Deep Water Royalty Relief Act, closing off arguments that the agency lacked that power.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that obtain federal leases after enactment would bear the cost, since royalty relief that is now granted without price limits would stop once production prices crossed the threshold, reducing their revenue from those leases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies on federal leases

drawbacks.text: Price limits on royalty relief could make deep-water drilling less attractive, and industry backers argue that relief is what encourages companies to take on the risk and expense of drilling in deep offshore waters, potentially reducing domestic production.
The bill applies only to leases entered into after enactment, so it would not recover royalties lost on leases already issued — meaning its financial benefit is prospective and gradual.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For taxpayers, the trade-off is favorable: the bill protects federal royalty revenue from leases signed at moments of high prices while leaving the relief tool available for genuinely marginal projects. The cost is that some deep-water drilling might become less profitable to pursue, a real but hard-to-quantify production effect, and the bill does nothing for the leases already in hand.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, so it died without ever coming to a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Kyl, joined by Sen. Mike DeWine, introduced the Royalty Relief Suspension Act of 2006 on July 27, 2006.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
The full action history shows no committee hearing, markup, or Senate floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land came out ahead: without any action on the bill, new leases could continue to carry royalty relief with no price limits, and the Treasury kept bearing the cost of royalty-free production during price spikes.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies on federal leases

for.name: Sen. Jon Kyl
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to attach price thresholds to royalty relief on new federal oil and gas leases.

for.name: Sen. Mike DeWine
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup appears in the record, so the Senate never voted on it.

against.name: Oil and gas producers on federal leases
against.role: Industry holding the royalty-relief benefit the bill would limit
against.what_they_did: Benefited from the continued availability of royalty relief without price thresholds; the bill's restriction was aimed squarely at this industry's federal lease terms.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls show the split; its two Senate supporters were both Republicans, but party positions were never tested.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal leases
industries.note: The bill would end royalty-free production on new federal leases once market prices crossed a threshold, directly cutting company revenue on those leases. That forgone royalty revenue is public money, so the industry's gain in this arrangement is the Treasury's and taxpayers' loss.

Leases under the Outer Continental Shelf Deep Water Royalty Relief Act rely on royalty suspensions; price thresholds would curtail that subsidy for high-price production. Drillers argue relief offsets the high cost and risk of deep-water operations.
